message.content:
The sea’s hue isn’t fixed—it shifts with depth, weather, time of day, and even what’s floating above it. In clear conditions at moderate depths (say up to 30 m), sunlight penetrates water but gets scattered more strongly in shorter wavelengths—blue light travels farther than reds or yellows. That selective absorption gives most people the classic “deep‑sea” blue you see in photographs.

But several other forces tug on that basic palette:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Depth** | Deeper waters absorb longer wavelengths first, so they look bluer. Shallow coastal zones often appear turquoise because green and yellow wavelengths still reach the surface. |
| **Sun angle & cloud cover** | A low sun near sunrise/sunset casts warm orange–red glints across calm seas, while overcast skies diffuse white light into a milky grayish tone. |
| **Water composition** | Suspended particles (silt, plankton) scatter all colors equally → murkier, brownish or greenish hues. Clear tropical lagoons may show vivid aquamarine due to minimal turbidity. |
| **Surface motion** | Calm waves reflect sky color; rough surf diffuses reflected rays, making the sea seem darker or grayer. |
| **Atmospheric pollution / aerosols** | Smog or dust can tint the ocean toward hazy greens or browns. |

So when someone says “the sea looks blue,” they’re usually referring to those deep‑water, sunny, relatively clean conditions where Rayleigh scattering dominates. But if you stand on a sandy beach during sunset, watch a storm roll in, or float among kelp forests, your perception will change dramatically—and that’s part of why we love looking out at the horizon!
